articles.title: Multidimensional vulnerabilities of informal settlements in the Urban South
articles.authors: Mingxing Chen, Wenming Song, Dadao Lu, Yu Deng, Chenglong Wang, Huiping Jiang, Yuyu Zhou, Murray W. Scown, Liangkan Chen, Jing Ma, Heran Zheng, Xuemei Bai
articles.abstract: Informal settlements are widespread and rapidly growing, often associated with high vulnerabilities. However, global-scale understanding on their spatial distribution and complexity of vulnerability is limited. Here, we delineate the informal settlements across a sample of 1,914 cities of the Global South by integrating Sentinel-2 imagery with deep learning models, and we explore the heterogeneity of vulnerability using Urban Informal Settlement Vulnerability Index that encompasses living conditions, social infrastructure, and environmental risk. We found that Urban Informal Settlements cover 12.94 ± 2.52% of their total urban areas (approximately 34.04 × 10 3 km 2 ), especially in sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, and Middle Asia. Sub-Saharan African cities have the highest vulnerability of informal settlements, with 31.75 ± 6.20% of total urban areas being occupied by informal settlements, while East Asian cities exhibit relatively low vulnerability across all dimensions. We also find that urban informal settlements with high environmental exposure are widespread in the Global South, and there is a significantly polarized distribution between “low” and “high” vulnerability categories. The findings highlight the disparate distribution of multidimensional vulnerability in informal settlements across the Urban South, providing a comparative evidence base for further local assessment and context-specific policy discussions related to SDG 11.

articles.title: Laundering and evasion in response to antislavery policies in Brazil’s cattle sector
articles.authors: Tara Mittelberg, Marin E. Skidmore, Juliana L. S. C. Brandão, Lisa L. Rausch, Holly K. Gibbs
articles.abstract: Modern slavery remains pervasive across many economic sectors. Progress toward eradicating it has been partially hindered by a lack of tested, comprehensive policy responses. Using data on millions of cattle transactions in Brazil, we evaluated how ranchers changed their selling behavior after being added to the “Dirty List,” a public registry that names and shames employers found to use modern slavery. Dirty Listed ranchers significantly reduced direct sales to slaughterhouses that signed sustainable supply chain commitments but evaded sanctions by laundering cattle through compliant intermediaries or selling to nonsignatory slaughterhouses. These responses weakened the financial cost of listing to ranchers, and likely allowed beef and leather linked to modern slave labor to enter international supply chains. Our findings highlight the limits of downstream enforcement and underscore the need to monitor upstream suppliers to ensure slavery-free supply chains.

articles.title: Reproducibility of social science research using aggregate statistics with noise infused for differential privacy
articles.authors: Ryan Steed, Eduardo Abraham Schnadower Mustri, Alessandro Acquisti
articles.abstract: Privacy-preserving analytics such as differential privacy are designed to allow the analysis of sensitive datasets while protecting individuals’ privacy. Their deployment, however, has been controversial. Critics maintain that statistical noise injected to preserve privacy can degrade the quality and feasibility of social science research. We select a benchmark of empirical findings from 93 published social science studies involving regression analyses over aggregate statistics. We evaluate whether their findings replicate on privacy noise-infused data. Under privacy budgets typical in industry, around 91% of simulated findings still support the original claims at significance level α = 0.1 . Claims based on weaker original effect sizes are more likely to be nullified or sometimes reversed. We compare distortions caused by privacy noise to those due to measurement errors and other kinds of nonsampling errors common in social statistics, and we find that the marginal impacts of privacy protection are smaller. Moreover, discrepancies due to privacy noise are often much smaller than discrepancies observed in traditional replication and robustness studies.

articles.title: AI-generated language remains systematically distinguishable from human communication
articles.authors: Nicolò Pagan, Petter Törnberg, Christopher A. Bail, Christopher Barrie
articles.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in the social sciences to simulate human behavior and communication, yet validation methods for these applications remain limited. Existing evaluations often rely on human judgments of plausibility, a coarse, difficult-to-scale, and often unreliable benchmark for distinguishing AI-generated from human text. As a result, researchers lack robust tools for assessing the realism of LLM-generated language and for calibrating models to real-world data. We address this gap in two ways. First, we introduce the Conversational Human Authenticity Test (CHAT), a validation framework that combines aggregate metrics of detectability and semantic similarity with interpretable linguistic features, including stylistic markers and topical patterns, to assess how closely LLMs approximate human language in a given dataset. Second, we benchmark nine open-weight LLMs across five calibration strategies, including fine-tuning, stylistic prompting, and context retrieval, on user interactions from X, Bluesky, and Reddit. We find that even after calibration, LLM outputs remain clearly distinguishable from human text, especially in affective tone and emotional expression. Instruction-tuned models generally underperform base models, and larger models do not obviously improve human-likeness. We also identify a trade-off between realism and semantic fidelity: methods that make outputs seem more human often move them further from the content of human responses. Together, these results provide a scalable framework for validation and calibration in LLM-based social simulation while underscoring current limits in reproducing human communication.

articles.title: Integrating cooperative breeding with reciprocity and culture extends Hamilton’s rule to humans
articles.authors: Alessandra Cassar, Daniel Friedman, Shreeja Guha, Timothy Wilkins
articles.abstract: We study how kinship and reciprocity shape giving and child care support in societies with limited access to markets. Extending Hamilton’s rule to incorporate reciprocity, we test it using behavioral data from dictator games and surveys in remote matrilocal and patrilocal villages of northeast India (N = 406 parents of young children). We replicate with data from urban Manila neighborhoods (N = 301) and the Solomon Islands (N = 624). Consistent with predictions, transfers to recipients increase with genetic relatedness to the donor and even more with relatedness to the donor’s child—a hallmark of reciprocity anchored in shared genetic investment. Nonanonymous conditions amplify giving, especially to nonkin. Cultural norms shape cooperation, but do not trump genetic relatedness. These results underscore the role of affinal ties and reciprocal exchange in sustaining cooperation, and suggest a mechanism through which cooperative breeding could contribute to the emergence of generalized reciprocity and human sociality.

articles_hidden.title: Improved assessment of Alaskan Arctic coastal wave exposure accounting for landfast ice
articles_hidden.authors: Martin Henke, Zhaoqing Yang, Ruth Branch
articles_hidden.abstract: Simulations of the ocean wave climate are critical for assessment of coastal processes and hazards in observation sparse regions such as the Arctic. While the multidecade wind and ice datasets necessary for driving long-term wave simulations have proven reliable for such efforts, the presence of landfast ice along shorelines at scales not represented by these data has been a persistent uncertainty impeding accurate analysis of impacts to Arctic coasts. Here, we explore this uncertainty by producing a historical high-resolution wave simulation and combining simulation outputs with landfast ice data for the Alaskan Arctic. The resulting dataset yields an improved assessment of coastal waves and identifies stark contrasts in the seasonal wave exposure of the Chukchi and Beaufort regions. Notably, analysis shows that absent supplemented landfast ice, coastal ice cover is broadly underestimated by 10 to 25 d, resulting in wave energy being overestimated by 5 to 10% in shallow depths nearshore. Notably, these figures can reach up to 70 d of underestimation for ice cover and 48% overestimation of wave energy in certain locations. The persistent overestimation and potential for extreme positive biases in coastal wave assessment highlight the need for representation of landfast ice in Arctic coastal analysis efforts and our analysis reveals the spatial and temporal biases for related research.

articles_hidden.title: Interventions to mitigate post-infection morbidity: Management insights from simple models
articles_hidden.authors: Prakhar Jaiswal, Daniel Coombs, Caroline E. Wagner, Troy Day, Chadi M. Saad-Roy
articles_hidden.abstract: A variety of pathogens that cause acute disease can also affect their host long after recovery. These post-infection effects lead to elevated costs for individuals and societies, which can be mitigated by large-scale interventions. Here, we examine the management of post-infection morbidity with mathematical models. First, we show that long-term usage of nonpharmaceutical interventions can reduce post-acute burden. Second, to investigate how post-infection effects affect optimal vaccination coverage, we generalize and expand on classic epidemiological-economic models. We include post-infection costs, and consider the cost of vaccination as a general increasing function of coverage. If there is some sub-elimination coverage that locally minimizes costs (beyond elimination), we show that the decision of whether to vaccinate or not is independent of the transmission rate (however elimination does depend on this). Echoing existing theoretical results with exponentially increasing costs, we find that if vaccination costs either only accelerate or only decelerate with increased coverage, there is a unique, transmission-independent interior level of vaccination coverage (nonzero and sub-elimination) that locally minimizes or maximizes societal costs, respectively. In all settings, we show that post-infection effects can substantially shift societal incentives toward elimination. Furthermore, when costs of vaccination change concavity, the optimal coverage level is very sensitive to post-infection costs: a small increase can shift optimal coverage from none (or low coverage) to elimination. Our findings demonstrate that post-infection morbidity has important implications for policy and management, and that there is an urgent need to quantify costs of post-infection effects and of large-scale vaccine deployment.

articles_hidden.title: Phylogenomics confirms Palaeoptera monophyly and illuminates the origin of winged insects
articles_hidden.authors: Shiyu Du, Yehao Wang, Feng Zhang, Michael S. Engel, Xuhongyi Zheng, Dewen Gong, Changfa Zhou, Chenyang Cai
articles_hidden.abstract: The origin and early radiation of winged insects (Pterygota) represent one of the most transformative events in terrestrial evolution, yet phylogenetic relationships among their basalmost lineages (Ephemeroptera, Odonata and Neoptera) continue to be a central debate within insect systematics. Here, we present the most taxonomically comprehensive phylogenomic analysis to date, leveraging genomic and transcriptomic data from 101 species, including 16 sequenced ephemeropteran genomes. Employing 1,367 universal single-copy orthologs across two supermatrices, we used concatenation- and coalescent-based frameworks under homogeneous and heterogeneous, and multispecies coalescent models. Our analyses support Palaeoptera monophyly. Although coalescent-based methods initially suggested a Chiastomyaria (Ephemeroptera + Neoptera) topology, subsequent signal dissection and topology tests confirm that the preponderance of genomic signal favors a monophyletic Palaeoptera. Furthermore, we identify incomplete lineage sorting and gene tree estimation error as the primary drivers of previous topological conflicts. Our molecular dating results point to an Early Devonian origin of crown-Pterygota, whereas crown-Palaeoptera first emerged in the Late Devonian. By reconciling molecular evidence with morphological synapomorphies, such as wing-base sclerite homologies, this study provides a coherent framework for the early evolution of winged insects, supports a single origin of wings, and identifies the neopteran wing-folding mechanism as a singular evolutionary innovation.

articles_hidden.title: Double periodicity of the AnkyrinG-associated complex in the axon initial segment
articles_hidden.authors: Gülberk Bayraktar, Josephine K. Dannersø, Sean D. S. Hansen, Lisbeth Schmidt Laursen, U. Valentin Nägerl, Poul Nissen
articles_hidden.abstract: The axon initial segment (AIS), situated within the first 20 to 60 µm of the axon, is essential for action potential generation and maintenance of axonal identity [M. N. Rasband, Nat. Rev. Neurosci. 11 , 552–562 (2010)]. Its structure relies on the beta (β)-IV-spectrin/AnkyrinG (AnkG) scaffold arranged periodically underneath the plasma membrane, harboring diverse membrane proteins [K. Xu, G. Zhong, X. Zhuang, Science 339 , 452–456 (2013); K. L. Hedstrom, Y. Ogawa, M. N. Rasband, J. Cell Biol. 183 , 635–640 (2008)]. Although a ~190-nm cytoskeletal periodic organization is well established, the precise stoichiometry and spatial arrangement of AIS proteins within the ~190-nm spatial period remain rudimentary, mostly for lack of sufficient spatial resolution and labeling efficiency. Here, using expansion microscopy and cryoelectron tomography, which overcome these technical limitations, we present data on the organization of the AnkG-associated complex within the ~190-nm spatial period. We demonstrate that exactly two AnkG molecules are situated within each period and with their C termini separated by ~80 nm. By contrast, the AnkG-associated cell-adhesion protein neurofascin-186 appears in clusters of varying sizes that are consistent with the periodic organization of AnkG pairs, yet suggesting a more complex molecular arrangement between the two molecules. Altogether, our approach provides insights into AIS molecular organization and protein stoichiometry.

articles_hidden.title: Convergent genome streamlining accompanies independent miniaturization in the world’s smallest fishes
articles_hidden.authors: Hiranya Sudasinghe, Michael Matschiner, Ralf Britz, Kevin W. Conway, Heok Hui Tan, Walter Salzburger, Catherine L. Peichel, Lukas Rüber
articles_hidden.abstract: Miniaturization, the reduction of adult body size to an extreme degree, has evolved repeatedly across vertebrates. Yet its genomic underpinnings remain poorly understood. Cypriniformes, the most species-rich order of freshwater fishes, contains multiple miniaturized lineages that have evolved via contrasting developmental processes. Proportioned dwarfs are tiny-bodied but otherwise morphologically similar to larger relatives, while progenetic miniatures exhibit developmental truncation and retain larval-like anatomical features into adulthood. Using a new time-calibrated phylogeny of 309 cypriniform species and comparative genomic analyses of 33 high-quality genome assemblies, we investigated the evolutionary history and genomic correlates of miniaturization across this order. Ancestral state reconstruction revealed multiple independent origins of both miniature types, with reversals to the nonminiature state rarely recovered and miniature origins nonrandomly distributed across the phylogeny. The origins of the two types of miniatures differed in their timing. Progenetic miniatures arose predominantly in the Eocene whereas proportioned dwarfs arose mainly within the Miocene period. Genome size variation across Cypriniformes has been overwhelmingly driven by polyploidy. However, progenetic miniatures showed a directionally consistent, though nonsignificant, trend toward genome size reduction. Comparative genomic analyses revealed that all three independently evolved progenetic miniature lineages share convergent signatures of repeat loss alongside genome-wide intron shortening, patterns absent in proportioned dwarfs. Our study provides the broadest evidence to date that progenetic miniaturization, despite independent origins, is underpinned by predictable structural genomic changes, revealing a fundamental link between developmental truncation and genome architecture in vertebrates.

articles_hidden.title: SETDB1 preferentially silences evolutionarily young retroelements
articles_hidden.authors: Bercin K. Cenik, Simai Wang, Marta Iwanaszko, Benjamin C. Howard, Irem Aydin, Sarah Gold, Vijay Ramani, Ali Shilatifard
articles_hidden.abstract: Transposable elements (TEs) are epigenetically silenced through multiple mechanisms, including heterochromatin formation and DNA methylation. Prior studies have implicated SETDB1 and the Human Silencing Hub (HUSH) complex in heterochromatin formation-based TE repression, but precise characterization of repeat subclass and locus-specific effects for SETDB1 and related mechanisms has been limited by short-read transcriptome mapping. Here, we use long-read RNA sequencing mapped to a telomere-to-telomere mouse genome assembly to resolve the specific contributions of SETDB1 to TE silencing at single-locus resolution. Knockdown of SETDB1 or core HUSH factors reveals robust and reproducible derepression of a restricted subset of long terminal repeat (LTR) retroelements distinct from those of global DNA demethylation. This derepression is heterogeneous within TE subclasses and is confined to discrete genomic loci, highlighting regulatory diversity that is obscured by aggregate, family-level analyses. Time-resolved SETDB1 depletion followed by histone 3 lysine 9 (H3K9)me3, H3K9me2, and Pol II ChIP-seq reveals a stratified derepression response: ERVK and ERV1 elements show concordant H3K9 methylation loss, Pol II gain, and RNA expression induction, consistent with direct H3K9me3-mediated silencing, whereas LINE/L1 elements show transcriptional activation without corresponding H3K9me3 loss, implicating parallel repressive mechanisms. These data support a model in which SETDB1-dependent H3K9 methylation maintains silencing of evolutionarily young LTRs, while long interspersed nuclear element (LINE) repression engages broader heterochromatic pathways not fully captured by any single chromatin readout. Collectively, our findings refine current models of heterochromatin-mediated TE control and provide a framework for dissecting how chromatin-based mechanisms cooperate to maintain subclass-selective TE repression.

articles_hidden.title: Shedding light on left hippocampal mGlu5 in Alzheimer’s disease
articles_hidden.authors: Charleine Zussy, Magalie Mathias, Mathieu Vitalis, Tristan Moujellil-Legagneur, Fanny Malhaire, Geoffrey Canet, Catherine Desrumaux, Sylvie Claeysen, Xavier Gómez-Santacana, Cyril Goudet, Amadeu Llebaria, Laurent Givalois
articles_hidden.abstract: Metabotropic glutamate receptor 5 (mGlu5) is essential for synaptic plasticity and memory, making it a potential therapeutic target in Alzheimer’s disease (AD). While hemispheric asymmetries in hippocampal function have been observed in AD patients, the lateralized contribution of mGlu5 signaling to cognitive decline remains unclear. Here, we show a physiological left-right asymmetry in hippocampal mGlu5 expression in wild-type mice, with higher levels in the left hemisphere, consistent with previous reports. This physiological asymmetry is lost in two distinct mouse models of AD, the J20 and 5xFAD mice, revealing a hemisphere-specific disruption of hippocampal mGlu5 regulation. Using the light-controllable negative allosteric modulator Alloswitch-1, we show that selective inhibition of left, but not right, hippocampal mGlu5 restores working and short-term memory in AD mice. This finding indicates that altered mGlu5 expression does not simply reflect receptor loss, but rather a dysregulated signaling state that remains functionally relevant and pharmacologically targetable. Left-specific modulation also normalizes pathological downstream signaling, including aberrant Pyk2 and GSK-3β activation and tau hyperphosphorylation, across both hemispheres, indicating a widespread impact of hemisphere-selective intervention. These findings establish a functional lateralization of hippocampal mGlu5 signaling and identify the left hippocampus as a critical site for mGlu5-dependent memory dysfunction in AD. They also highlight the therapeutic potential of region-specific photopharmacology for precise intervention in early AD pathology, providing a strategy for spatially targeted modulation of pathological synaptic signaling in neurodegenerative disease.

articles_hidden.title: Discovery and characterization of miranthins, “Trojan horse” antibiotic modulators of bacterial composition in the oral microbiome
articles_hidden.authors: Brielle E. Dalvano, Brett C. Covington, Mohammad R. Seyedsayamdost
articles_hidden.abstract: Bacteria of the human microbiota encode an abundance of natural products that likely mediate bacterial competition, local colonization patterns, and human health and disease. However, very few of these compounds have been identified and characterized to date. During our investigation of Streptococcus mitis , an important early colonizer of the oral cavity, we identified and structurally characterized a family of peptide natural products, termed miranthins herein, that contain an unusual macrocycle formed by an Asp-Cys β-carbon thioether crosslink. We determined that the most abundantly secreted miranthin is a “Trojan horse” antibiotic that enters sensitive cells via the Ami oligopeptide transporter, is hydrolyzed and activated by aminopeptidase N, and subsequently inhibits ribosomal translation to curb the growth of streptococcal competitors. The miranthins are narrow-spectrum antibiotics that could enable S. mitis to modulate community dynamics in the oral cavity, highlighting the importance of peptide natural products in interspecies competition in the microbiome.

articles_hidden.title: Multiyear dual-isotope fingerprinting at South Asian receptor sites constrains carbon monoxide sources and enhanced oxidation
articles_hidden.authors: Peng Yao, Henry Holmstrand, Carina van der Veen, Maria Elena Popa, Chloe A. Brashear, Krishnakant Budhavant, Mohanan Remani Manoj, Joakim Romson, Abdus Salam, Thomas Röckmann, Örjan Gustafsson
articles_hidden.abstract: Carbon monoxide (CO) is an indirect short-lived climate forcer with uncertainties both in sources and its role in atmospheric oxidation. Based on nine winter-long dual-isotope campaigns at two South Asian receptor sites intercepting the continental outflow, we quantified CO source contributions and emission–sink dynamics. Combustion accounts for 68 to 74% of South Asia regional CO (including 34 to 37% from biomass burning) with secondary atmospheric oxidation contributing 26 to 32% (dominated by oxidation of nonmethane volatile organic compounds (NMVOCs) at 21 to 26%, with methane oxidation contributing 5.5 to 6.4%). These isotope-observational constraints suggest a twice higher role for atmospheric oxidation than in model estimates. Spatially, the absolute contributions of both primary and secondary CO decrease from the Indo-Gangetic Plain to the northern Indian Ocean, while the relative contribution of oxidation-derived CO increases, indicating enhanced secondary CO production near source regions. Observation-model comparison suggests that transport from the continental areas dominates CO over adjacent oceanic regions, with minor local production. During the COVID-19 emission perturbation, combustion-derived CO fell sharply in absolute terms, NMVOC-derived CO rose, and CH 4 -derived CO remained stable, providing an observational constraint on the sensitivity of atmospheric oxidation to emission changes. Our results reveal a significant contribution of CO from atmospheric oxidation in South Asia, calling for a reassessment of regional emission–oxidation coupling in models and of mitigation strategies.

articles_hidden.title: Nutrient legacies from elephant megacarcasses create coldspots of biodiversity and hotspots of ecosystem processes
articles_hidden.authors: Courtney G. Reed, Nathan P. Lemoine, Michelle L. Budny, Vincent C. Clarke, Johan T. du Toit, Ryan Helcoski, Helga Knoetze, Jane M. Lucas, Joshua P. Schimel, Izak P. J. Smit, Tercia Strydom, Aimee G. Tallian, Dave I. Thompson, Deron E. Burkepile
articles_hidden.abstract: Terrestrial megafauna (animals >1,000 kg) have substantial impacts on ecosystems while alive; yet, we know little about the impacts of these ecosystem engineers after they die. Like whale carcasses in the ocean, terrestrial megacarcasses may leave ecological legacies via the nutrient pulses they create on the landscape. Here, we investigated the impact of elephant megacarcasses on savanna ecosystems in Kruger National Park, South Africa. To determine how elephant carcasses affect below- and aboveground biodiversity and ecosystem processes, we collected soil and plant samples from 40 carcass sites (pairing “on carcass” and “off carcass” samples) ranging from 8 d to 7.7 y postmortem. We found that elephant carcasses released enormous pools of nutrients into savanna soils, increasing ammonium by 31×, nitrate by 7×, and phosphorus by 3× on average. These extreme ammonium concentrations were negatively correlated with the biodiversity of bacteria and plants, which were both suppressed at elephant carcass sites. Despite these decreases in biodiversity, ecosystem processes were strongly elevated at elephant carcass sites, with soil microbial respiration elevated for 1 to 2 y and herbivore grazing >3× higher for 7+ y postmortem. These results demonstrate that elephant megacarcasses generate coldspots of biodiversity but hotspots of ecosystem processes, unveiling a cryptic ecological function of megaherbivores that is extreme in both magnitude and duration relative to carcasses of smaller animals. As humans drive terrestrial megafauna toward extinction, we risk losing not only their ecosystem engineering abilities while they are alive but also the ecological legacies their carcasses create after death.

articles_hidden.title: P-body-mediated RNA decay controls neural crest EMT
articles_hidden.authors: Arvind Arul Nambi Rajan, Michael L. Piacentino, Marianne E. Bronner, Erica J. Hutchins
articles_hidden.abstract: Neural crest cells, a multipotent vertebrate stem cell population, undergo a tightly regulated epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT) to delaminate from the neural tube and initiate migration. Neural crest EMT is controlled by a transient pulse of Draxin , which acts as a molecular rheostat of canonical Wnt signaling, and is then rapidly downregulated by unknown mechanisms. To address this, here we use in vivo reporter assays and live RNA imaging to show that Draxin mRNA is rapidly degraded posttranscriptionally via its 3′ untranslated region. We found that Draxin transcripts are targeted to cytoplasmic processing bodies (P-bodies), which are membrane-less sites of RNA processing and decay. Disruption of P-bodies by CRISPR/Cas9-mediated depletion of the RNA helicase DDX6 prevented posttranscriptional downregulation of Draxin and impaired neural crest EMT in vivo. These findings parallel observations in human patients carrying DDX6 mutations, who exhibit defects in P-body assembly and craniofacial abnormalities associated with neural crest dysfunction. Together, our results identify P-bodies as regulators of Draxin mRNA decay and reveal a spatially organized mechanism of RNA turnover that controls neural crest EMT during vertebrate development.

articles_hidden.title: A multiscale framework for heme crystallization inhibition: From single-molecule step-capping to parasite suppression
articles_hidden.authors: Huan-Jui Lee, Sandra Massih, Mahnoor Abdullah, Hariharan Annadurai, Jeffrey D. Rimer, David J. Sullivan, Peter G. Vekilov
articles_hidden.abstract: Heme crystallization is central to malaria parasites’ survival during the erythrocytic stage of the disease, yet how clinically relevant antimalarial drugs modulate this process at the molecular level remains unclear. Here we employ stage-resolved parasite assays and multiscale in vitro approaches to explore the interactions between lumefantrine (LF), one of the popular components of current combination therapies, and hematin crystallization. Pulse LF suppresses Plasmodium falciparum during both ring and trophozoite stages. Under biomimetic conditions, LF markedly reduces β-hematin crystal growth rates. High-resolution atomic force microscopy reveals that individual LF molecules bind directly to crystal steps, physically constraining step motion through a previously unreported step-capping mechanism. This localized inhibition propagates to the mesoscale, producing step broadening, reduced interstep spacing, and causing surface kinetic roughening. In contrast to its strong inhibition of crystal growth, LF enhances hematin nucleation by promoting the formation of mesoscopic hematin-rich clusters, as detected by a combination of scattering and microscopy techniques. Attachment of the nucleated crystallites to larger crystal surfaces initiates a nonclassical inhibition sequence by straining the crystal interface, which further impedes step growth.

articles_hidden.title: Dystrophic changes of nigrostriatal axons harboring a SYNJ1 Parkinson’s mutation suggest catastrophic failure of endocytic mechanisms
articles_hidden.authors: Yumei Wu, Peng Xu, James Moran, C. Shan Xu, Kenneth J. Hayworth, Mian Cao, Lin Shao, D. James Surmeier, Harald F. Hess, Pietro De Camilli
articles_hidden.abstract: Synaptojanin 1 is a brain enriched phosphoinositide phosphatase implicated in endocytosis at the synapse. A mutation (R258Q) that selectively impairs its Sac1 phosphatase domain causes early onset familial Parkinsonism. Neurons of mice with this mutation display synaptic vesicle traffic defects across the brain, but selective dystrophic changes in a subset of dopaminergic axons in the dorsolateral striatum. Using correlative light microscopy-FIB-SEM of mutant mouse striata to visualize in 3D these abnormal structures we show that they represent clusters of focal axonal dilations harboring massive, onion-like DAT enriched plasma membrane infoldings, generally localized next to cell bodies of neighboring cells, often engulfing evaginations of such cells. This dysmorphia was associated with a deficit in dopamine release in the same striatal region. Given the involvement of Synj1 in endocytic mechanisms, these structures may reflect an imbalance between exocytosis and endocytosis. Their occurrence only in a subset of axons suggests a vulnerability threshold of these axons beyond which the expansion of the plasma membrane is not counteracted by compensatory mechanisms.

articles_hidden.title: Transcriptional regulation and function of GPR18 in macrophage subtype specification
articles_hidden.authors: Hebe Agustina Mena, Andreas Patsalos, Jake Altomare, Filippa Davidsson, Gergely Nagy, Wilhelm K. Berger, Blenda Wong, Allison Rahtes, Gabrielle Fredman, Laszlo Nagy, Matthew Spite
articles_hidden.abstract: Resolution of inflammation is mediated in part by agonists that engage immune cells to dampen inflammatory signaling, promote phagocytic functions, and facilitate tissue repair. G protein–coupled receptor 18 (GPR18) has emerged as an important proresolving receptor that is activated by endogenous mediators including Resolvin D2. However, very little is known about how GPR18 expression is controlled in immune cells, and its cell-autonomous roles during resolution of inflammation remain of interest. Here, we elucidated transcriptional and epigenetic regulation of Gpr18 in macrophages (MFs). We identified binding of monocyte/macrophage lineage-determining transcription factors (LDTFs) including PU.1, IRF8, and RUNX1 at the Gpr18 locus in the basal state in murine bone marrow–derived macrophages (BMDM). We found that Gpr18 is highly induced in BMDM by inflammatory stimuli including interferon gamma (IFNγ) and ligands for multiple toll-like receptors. Motif analysis predicted enrichment for LDTFs and signal-dependent TFs including nuclear factor κB (NFκB) and interferon regulatory factors (IRF) at the Gpr18 locus. Stimulation of BMDM with lipopolysaccharide (LPS) or IFNγ increased the binding of NFκB p65 and IRF1 at the Gpr18 locus, which played a causal role in the induction of Gpr18 by LPS or IFNγ, respectively. Mice with myeloid deficiency of Gpr18 had increased tissue swelling and accumulation of “inflammatory” Ly6C hi monocytes/MFs during contact hypersensitivity, which was recapitulated during acute peritonitis and led to altered transcriptomes of resolution-phase MFs. These results demonstrate that inflammatory signaling primes MFs for resolution in part by inducing Gpr18 , which plays a cell-autonomous role to regulate MF phenotypic transitions.

articles_hidden.title: Multiple-oxygen isotope constraints on aerobic respiration and gross primary productivity
articles_hidden.authors: Eleanor R. Hughes, Kevin M. Sutherland, David T. Johnston
articles_hidden.abstract: Primary production on land and in the surface ocean is a critical component of Earth’s carbon and oxygen cycles, controlling the uptake of CO 2 and the release of O 2 to the atmosphere. Quantitative estimates of these O 2 and CO 2 fluxes remain challenging. Of the methods used, the triple-oxygen-isotope analysis of O 2 is considered to provide the most robust in situ estimate of gross productivity. However, this method relies on one key assumption—that the oxygen isotope fractionation of aerobic respiration is constant—and recent experimental studies have shown that it can vary significantly. When applied to the same calculation of gross productivity, the experimentally determined variation in fractionation could produce > 100% error. In this work, the mechanistic origin of the variation in respiratory fractionation is explored using experiments on the model organism Escherichia coli . These experiments suggest that the fractionation is strongly correlated with the cell-specific O 2 consumption rate, weakly correlated with the dissolved-O 2 concentration, and may also depend on the identity of the terminal oxidase enzyme used to reduce O 2 . Modeling suggests that these influences on fractionation are likely to be important in the marine water column, and could produce up to ± 120% error in estimates of gross productivity made using triple-oxygen-isotope analyses. This error may be significantly reduced through concurrent analyses of the “clumped” (multiply substituted) isotopologue abundances in O 2 .

articles_hidden.title: Autoimmunity induced by epigenome alteration affecting thymic Treg cell development
articles_hidden.authors: Jia Long, Jun Huang, Masaya Arai, Yamami Nakamura, Norihisa Mikami, Kenji Ichiyama, Shimon Sakaguchi
articles_hidden.abstract: Methyl-CpG-binding domain protein 3 (MBD3), an essential component of the nucleosome remodeling and deacetylase (NuRD) complex, controls chromatin accessibility at lineage-specific transcriptional enhancers and promoters during hematopoietic cell differentiation. Here, we have shown that MBD3 deficiency in the T cell compartment resulted in spontaneous development of T cell–mediated multiorgan autoimmune diseases including fatal autoimmune myocarditis. The MBD3-deficient mice notably showed a significant reduction of CD25 + Foxp3 + regulatory T (Treg) cells in both the thymus and periphery without much affecting the development and function of conventional T (Tconv) cells. Mixed bone marrow (BM) chimeras reconstituted with wild-type and MBD3-deficient BM revealed a cell-intrinsic defect in thymic Treg cell lineage differentiation in MBD3-deficient cells. Transcriptional, phenotypic, and functional analyses of thymocyte subsets further revealed that MBD3 deficiency particularly affected the activation of a Treg-specific enhancer of the Il2ra gene encoding CD25, hence impaired CD25 expression in immature CD4 single-positive thymocytes (ImCD4SP) but not in peripheral T cells. The impairment markedly limited thymic Treg precursor cell generation and substantially reduced overall thymic Treg cell output. By contrast, MBD3 deficiency scarcely impacted the TGF-β/IL-2-dependent in vitro Treg cell generation from Tconv cells. Thus, Treg-specific developmental properties such as high IL-2/CD25 dependency of their thymic differentiation may render them more sensitive than Tconv cells to epigenetic changes of the whole T cell compartment. The results provide a mechanistic basis by which general epigenomic alterations in the T cell compartment can be causative of autoimmune and other immunological diseases through selectively affecting thymic Treg cell development.

articles_hidden.title: Reaction-based cryo-EM resolves the continuous conformational spectrum of CTP synthase catalysis
articles_hidden.authors: Chen-Jun Guo, Yu-Fen Wu, Shu-Ying Guo, You Fu, Wei Wang, Ji-Long Liu
articles_hidden.abstract: Capturing enzymes under native turnover conditions remains a grand challenge in structural biology. Here, we develop a reaction-based cryo–electron microscopy (cryo-EM) strategy that directly samples Drosophila melanogaster cytidine triphosphate synthase (CTPS) from actively catalyzing mixtures containing only natural substrates and allosteric effectors. By integrating reaction-based sampling with three-dimensional variability analysis, we resolve a continuous conformational spectrum of CTPS during catalysis. This approach visualizes the chemical progression of 4-phosphoryl-uridine triphosphate (4Pi-UTP) formation and reveals a previously unobserved co-occupancy pattern of adenosine triphosphate (ATP) and CTP at the reaction end point. Cross-validation with nonhydrolyzable ATP analogs demonstrates that UTP phosphorylation by ATP, rather than mere ATP binding, shifts the conformational ensemble toward more closed states. Our findings establish reaction-based cryo-EM as a framework for resolving chemically annotated conformational ensembles without predefining a single trapped intermediate.

articles_hidden.title: Efficient and robust control with spikes that constrain free energy
articles_hidden.authors: André Urbano, Pablo Lanillos, Sander Keemink
articles_hidden.abstract: Animal brains exhibit remarkable efficiency in perception and action, while being robust to both external and internal perturbations. The means by which brains accomplish this remains, for now, poorly understood, hindering our understanding of animal and human cognition, as well as our own implementation of efficient algorithms for control of dynamical systems. A potential candidate for a robust mechanism of state estimation and action computation is the free energy principle, but existing implementations of this principle have largely relied on conventional, biologically implausible approaches without spikes. We propose an efficient and robust spiking control framework with realistic biological characteristics. The resulting networks function as free energy constrainers, in which neurons only fire if they reduce the free energy of their internal representation. The networks offer efficient operation through highly sparse activity while matching performance with other similar spiking frameworks, and have high resilience against both external (e.g., sensory noise or collisions) and internal perturbations (e.g., synaptic noise and delays or neuron silencing) that such a network would be faced with when deployed by either an organism or an engineer. Overall, our work provides a mathematical account for spiking control through constraining free energy, providing both better insight into how brain networks might leverage their spiking substrate and a route for implementing efficient control algorithms in neuromorphic hardware.

articles_hidden.title: Understanding consciousness (biological and artificial) as a society of self-schemas
articles_hidden.authors: Michael S. A. Graziano
articles_hidden.abstract: This article argues that human cognition is more than the performance of functions such as memory, decision-making, and attention. The brain also builds schematic models of those cognitive functions and uses those models to monitor, predict, and partially control them. When you introspect, your understanding of who you are and what is happening inside of you is derived from those schematic, sometimes inaccurate, but generally useful models, rather than from the actual cognitive functions that are represented by those models. The proposal expands the previously proposed attention schema theory to a more general schema theory, in which the mind as we know it introspectively is a society of interacting self-schemas. The article focuses on five self-schemas including the attention schema (which is proposed to give us our intuitions about a conscious mind that takes possession of items in a vivid manner), a decision schema (which generates simplified, sometimes confabulated accounts of the decision-making process and gives us our intuitive understanding of agency and will), emotion schemas (which create complex interpretations of the physiological state of the body and provide us with our understanding of emotional experience), the body schema (which provides our understanding of who we are as physical beings), and personas (which give us our understanding of our emotional, social, and moral character, and act as a framework to guide our behavior). The article includes a discussion of how consciousness in a machine requires a similar suite of self-schemas used for similar functional purposes and may already be partially present.

articles_hidden.title: Shading enhances Se accumulation in tea leaves through promoting CsMYB7-like-mediated conversion of Se (VI) to Se (IV)
articles_hidden.authors: Jianhui Ye, An Yan, Qiting Fang, Yijie Liu, Chunyang Li
articles_hidden.abstract: Limited selenium (Se) accumulation in agricultural products contributes to widespread dietary Se deficiency, posing a global nutritional threat. Efficient agronomic strategies to enhance Se biofortification in crops are still lacking. Here, we reveal the synergistic effects of shading and Se nanoparticles application on Se biofortification in tea leaves. Field experiments demonstrate that shading enhances Se accumulation in tea leaves under sufficient Se supply, through activating Se metabolism pathway. We identify CsAPR1 functions at the early stage of Se assimilation, catalyzing the reduction of Se (VI). The transcription of CsAPR1 is activated by CsMYB7-like and is further promoted by shading through interaction with CsbHLH70. Under sunlight, CsHY5 competes with CsbHLH70 for binding to CsMYB7-like, thereby attenuating CsMYB7-like-mediated transcription of CsAPR1 and suppressing Se accumulation in tea plants. Our findings reveal the molecular mechanisms underlying shade-induced enhancement of Se biofortification, offering insights and strategies for Se-enriched crop production.

articles_hidden.title: In mice, a population of male germ cells show characteristics of nonapoptotic cell death during G0 arrest
articles_hidden.authors: Kara Stark, Talia Hatkevich, Edward A. Miao, Tomokazu Souma, Blanche Capel
articles_hidden.abstract: In mammals, a small population of spermatogonial stem cells (SSCs) is established shortly after birth. These cells self-renew and produce sperm for the male’s reproductive lifespan, passing the genome on to the next generation. Establishment of a population of SSCs with high genomic integrity is essential. SSCs are derived from a much larger precursor population of male germ cells (MGCs) that differentiate during fetal life. During the last third of gestation, MGCs undergo a prolonged period of G0 cell cycle arrest during which they sustain high levels of transcription and acquire epigenetic programming for SSC fate. Although these differentiation steps can cause cellular and genomic damage, it has been unclear whether selection for germ cell quality occurs during G0 arrest since no classic markers of cell death have been detected. In this study, we used a mouse model to characterize a population of MGCs that begin to accumulate markers of cell death, such as AnnexinV (AnV) and propidium iodide (PI), at E16.5. The AnV- and PI-positive MGC population is characterized by low expression of the RNA-binding protein, Dead End 1, and exhibits dsDNA breaks and mitochondrial dysfunction. Interestingly, we do not see evidence of an active cell death cascade until the time of birth, when phosphorylation of MLKL, a hallmark of necroptotic cell death, occurs. Based on these findings, we propose that variable cellular health is an important basis for selection of SSC precursors.

articles_hidden.title: Quantum Fisher information and photon statistics from shift current shot noise
articles_hidden.authors: Evgenii Barts, Takahiro Morimoto, Naoto Nagaosa
articles_hidden.abstract: Quantum Fisher information (QFI) sets the ultimate precision of optical phase measurements and can reveal multiphoton entanglement. Yet the photon-number fluctuations that encode this sensitivity are difficult to convert into an electrical signal. We theoretically predict that a photodetector utilizing the shot noise of the quantum-geometric shift current of exciton polaritons can measure photon-number statistics and, for pure states, infer the QFI. By solving the Lindblad equation, we obtain the time-dependent nonlinear photocurrent for an arbitrary initial photon state. It turns out that, regardless of the quantum state of the incident light, the integrated current depends only on the mean photon number. In contrast, the shot noise retains information about photon-number fluctuations: Its Fano factor is proportional to the photon-number variance. Numerical calculations confirm these relations for optical Schrödinger cat and squeezed-vacuum states. A photodetector based on shift current noise can therefore provide a solid-state platform for high-precision measurements of quantum-optical statistics without relying on mobile photocarriers.

articles_hidden.title: Ice-ray pentagonal packing of pseudo-fivefold helices
articles_hidden.authors: Lida Aeindartehran, Luke Kwan, Ibrahim Tahir, Daniel K. Unruh, Maria Petrov, William B. Stoll, Alejandro Alvarez, Jia-Sen Hu, Ejaz Ahmed, Nilanjan Seal, Nathan Taton, Anja Milenkova, Robert E. Dinnebier, Murillo Longo Martins, Yongqiang Cheng, Anibal J. Ramirez-Cuesta, Jin S. Zhang, Michael T. Ruggiero, Panče Naumov, Tomče Runčevski
articles_hidden.abstract: While fivefold point symmetry is common in nature, fivefold spatial symmetry is seldom observed. Regular pentagons cannot tile a plane without leaving voids, and even the densest “ice-ray” packing is exceptionally rare. Fivefold helices are equally elusive. We report a small molecule that self-assembles into hydrogen-bonded pseudo-fivefold helices and adopts an ice-ray pentagonal packing motif over crystallographic length scales using peripheral disorder that partially occupies regions that would otherwise be void in an ideal pentagonal tessellation. The resulting structure exhibits weak and nondirectional interhelical interactions within the ( bc ) plane and comparatively strong and directional intrahelical hydrogen bonding along the a axis. This structural anisotropy gives rise to single crystals with large aspect ratios and distinct mechanical behavior. This realization of two rare structural motifs within a single crystal shows the capability of simple organic molecules to form complex structures and highlights an untapped potential for symmetry engineering in molecular solids through the interplay of intermolecular interactions with pronounced differences in strength and directionality.

articles_hidden.title: Heterochronicity shapes brain network formation
articles_hidden.authors: Francesco Poli, Stuart Oldham, Alexa Mousley, Edward T. Bullmore, Petra E. Vértes, Duncan E. Astle
articles_hidden.abstract: Brain network formation unfolds on a nonuniform developmental timetable, with different cortical regions generating connections at different developmental phases. Generative network models (GNMs) aim to uncover the principles underpinning the organization of connectomes by creating synthetic networks according to simple computational rules. These models capture the connectome’s topology, operationalized here as the cumulative distributions of network metrics (e.g., modularity, small-worldness, rich-club structure). However, GNMs typically ignore the differential timing of connectivity formation, and by omitting this temporal programme they often misplace topological features in physical space. Here, we add a heterochronous growth term to GNMs and use a model fitness function that weighs topology and topography equally. Topography refers to the spatial embedding of the network—the actual anatomical positions of the axonal tracts. With these advances, we can generate synthetic networks that more faithfully reproduce the spatial layout of diffusion-MRI connectomes from two independent adult cohorts. Compared with classical, temporally agnostic models, heterochronous simulations improve model fit, accurately locate cortical hubs and modules across individuals, and converge on a single caudal-to-rostral gradient of brain maturation. Overall, integrating heterochronicity makes GNMs more faithful to brain development, and allows for better identification of individual differences in network formation.

articles_hidden.title: Coordinated transformations of the labyrinth and occiput during the dinosaur–bird transition
articles_hidden.authors: Guillermo Navalón, Serjoscha W. Evers, Emma Hughes, Alexander Bjarnason, Luis M. Chiappe, Stig A. Walsh, James M. Neenan, Elsa Panciroli, Daniel J. Field, Roger B. J. Benson
articles_hidden.abstract: Evolutionary shape changes of the vertebrate semicircular canals (SCCs) are often ascribed to evolutionary transitions in locomotion, including the origin of flight during the dinosaur–bird transition. However, the potential for transformations of braincase architecture to influence SCC shape independent of sensory-functional adaptation has generally been overlooked. We evaluate the influence of both factors using a large dataset of 146 living and recently extinct crown birds, including taxa representing ~24 independent evolutionary losses of flight, together with Mesozoic stem avialans, nonavialan dinosaurs, and pterosaurs. Among crown birds, evolutionary changes in locomotor capabilities, including the total loss of flight, have only weak effects on SCC shape, contrasting with large effects from changes in braincase geometry. Notably, rotation of the occiput toward a ventral orientation is associated with important changes to SCC shape that match those observed during the dinosaur–bird transition. This suggests that evolutionary transformations of SCC shape during the Mesozoic origin of avian flight resulted from evolutionary changes in the orientation of the craniocervical joint, and not from tuning of SCC sensory function. These findings illuminate the importance of integrated morphological changes to the head-neck system during bird origins and challenge the long-standing assumption that SCC morphology enables confident inferences of the locomotor capabilities of extinct vertebrates.

articles_hidden.title: Learning dissipative chaotic dynamics with boundedness guarantees
articles_hidden.authors: Sunbochen Tang, Themistoklis P. Sapsis, Navid Azizan
articles_hidden.abstract: Chaotic dynamics, commonly seen in weather systems and fluid turbulence, are characterized by their sensitivity to initial conditions, which makes accurate prediction challenging. Recent approaches have focused on developing data-driven models that attempt to preserve invariant statistics over long horizons since many chaotic systems exhibit dissipative behaviors and ergodicity. Despite the recent progress in such models, they are still often prone to generating unbounded trajectories, leading to invalid statistics evaluation. To address this fundamental challenge, we introduce a modular framework that provides formal guarantees of trajectory boundedness for neural network chaotic dynamics models. Our core contribution is a dissipative projection layer that leverages control-theoretic principles to ensure the learned system is dissipative. Specifically, our framework simultaneously learns a dynamics emulator and an energy-like function, where the latter is used to construct an algebraic dissipative constraint within the projection layer. Furthermore, the learned invariant level set provides an outer estimate for the system’s strange attractor, which is known to be difficult to characterize due to its complex geometry. We demonstrate our model’s ability to produce bounded long-horizon forecasts that preserve invariant statistics for chaotic dynamical systems, including Lorenz 96 and a reduced-order model of the Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equation.

articles_hidden.title: Mechanisms of intracellular pH gating and local anesthetic inhibition of the two-pore domain K + channel TASK-2
articles_hidden.authors: Trevor Docter, Ben Sorum, Baobin Li, Robert A. Rietmeijer, Annan S. I. Cook, Abhay Kotecha, Stephen G. Brohawn
articles_hidden.abstract: TWIK-related acid-sensitive K+ channel 2 (TASK-2) is a pH sensing two-pore K + (K2P) channel that regulates respiration in brainstem neurons and systemic pH homeostasis in kidney. Despite its physiological importance and implication in disease, the molecular basis for intracellular gating and pharmacological inhibition of TASK-2 is incompletely understood. Here, we combine cryo-EM and single-channel electrophysiology to resolve the mechanisms of TASK-2 gating by intracellular protons and inhibition by the anesthetic bupivacaine. We show protonation of intracellular lysines triggers a unique stacked gating mechanism distinct from other K + channels. Inner helices unwind and domain swap to form a β-zipper, which we call a Z-gate, that seals the cytoplasmic channel entrance. These conformational changes open lateral fenestrations to the membrane that permit lipids to invade the channel cavity and block the pore. Furthermore, we find bupivacaine inhibits the channel by competing with lipids in the cavity site in a state-dependent manner. These results define a paradigm for intracellular gating of K2Ps and provide a structural foundation for designing more potent and selective channel modulators.

articles_hidden.title: Antiferromagnetism and tightly bound Cooper pairs induced by kinetic frustration
articles_hidden.authors: Yixin Zhang, Cristian D. Batista, Yang Zhang
articles_hidden.abstract: Antiferromagnetism and superconductivity are often viewed as competing orders in correlated electron systems. Here, we demonstrate that kinetic frustration in hole motion facilitates their coexistence within the square-lattice repulsive Hubbard model. Combining exact analytical solutions on tailored geometries with large-scale numerical simulations, we reveal a robust pairing mechanism: Holes on opposite sublattices behave as if they carry opposite effective charges due to spin singlet formation from kinetic frustration. This emergent property suppresses phase separation and fosters a coherent d -wave superconducting channel embedded within a long-range antiferromagnetic background. Our findings establish a minimal yet broadly applicable framework for stabilizing strong-coupling superconductivity in doped Mott insulators.

articles_hidden.title: A second-generation “hypoxia in a pill” rescues neurodegenerative phenotypes across distinct mouse models
articles_hidden.authors: Hong Wang, Eizo Marutani, Luca Zazzeron, Marissa Menard, Laura Volpicelli-Daley, Fumito Ichinose, Vamsi K. Mootha
articles_hidden.abstract: A growing body of preclinical research is demonstrating the therapeutic potential of chronic, continuous hypoxia (11% FIO 2 ) for rare and common diseases. However, the chronic delivery of hypoxic gas poses both practical challenges and long-term safety concerns. We previously introduced a small-molecule, “hypoxia-in-a-pill” combining a hemoglobin affinity enhancer (GBT440) to limit oxygen delivery with a HIF-2α inhibitor (PT2399) to prevent detrimental compensatory erythropoiesis. Although this small-molecule regimen extended the lifespan of the Ndufs4 knockout (KO) mouse model of mitochondrial complex I deficiency and Leigh syndrome, its efficacy did not match chronic 11% FIO 2 . Here we optimize this regimen using GBT601, a second-generation hemoglobin affinity enhancer with longer half-life and greater hemoglobin occupancy, and show it rescues key neurodegenerative phenotypes in multiple models. When we initiate therapy in 50 d old Ndufs4 KO mice with advanced disease, GBT601 monotherapy alleviated neurological disease phenotypes and extended median lifespan from 62 to 105 d, while dual therapy with the GBT601/PT2399 combination extended median lifespan to 158 d. When initiated after onset of advanced disease in a mouse model of Friedreich’s ataxia, the combination halted further progression of motor phenotypes. In a mouse model of Parkinson’s disease due to α-synuclein toxicity, initiating the GBT601/PT2399 combination after onset of motor dysfunction attenuates brain hyperoxia and lipid peroxidation and reverses motor phenotypes. Importantly, the combination maintained body weight without inducing any signs of pulmonary hypertension. Our findings motivate further preclinical and clinical evaluation of our “hypoxia in a pill” approach for diseases with high unmet need.

articles_hidden.title: Spatiotemporal noise stabilizes unbounded diversity in strongly competitive communities
articles_hidden.authors: Amer Al-Hiyasat, Daniel W. Swartz, Jeff Gore, Mehran Kardar
articles_hidden.abstract: Classical ecological models predict that diverse communities should be unstable, presenting a central challenge to explaining the stable biodiversity seen in nature. We revisit this long-standing problem by extending the generalized Lotka–Volterra model to include both spatial structure and environmental fluctuations across space and time. We find that neither space nor environmental noise alone can resolve the tension between diversity and stability, but that together they permit arbitrarily many species to stably coexist in a sufficiently large system, despite strongly disordered competitive interactions. We analytically characterize the noise-induced transition to coexistence, showing that spatiotemporal noise drives power-law abundance fluctuations, leading to an anomalous scaling of moments known empirically as Taylor’s law. At the metacommunity level, this manifests as an emergent sublinear self-inhibition that stabilizes diversity and renders the interaction disorder irrelevant in the high-diversity limit. Spatiotemporal noise thus provides a resolution to the diversity-stability paradox and a generic mechanism by which complex communities can persist.
